Suggest a reason why the supermarket should not test all the avocados in the delivery.

The supermarket tests a sample of 5 avocados and finds that 4 of them are ripe. They estimate that 80% of the avocados in the deliver are ripe. Suggest one way that the supermarket could improve their estimate.

1. A school uses a census to investigate the dietary requirements of its students.
(a) Explain what is meant by a census.
(b) Give one advantage and one disadvantage to the school of using a census.
A census observes or measures every member of a population.
It gives a completely accurate result.
A disadvantage could be either of the following.
2. A factory makes safety harnesses for climbers and has an order to supply 3000 harnesses. The buyer wishes to know that the load at which the harness breaks exceeds a certain figure.
(a) Suggest a reason why a census would not be used for this purpose.
The factory tests four harnesses and records their breaking loads.
(b) The factory claims that the harnesses are safe for loads up to 250 kg. Use the sample data to comment on this claim.
(c) Suggest one way in which the company can improve its prediction.
Testing destroys the harness. A census would destroy every harness, leaving none for climbers to use.
The claim is misleading. The mean and median breaking loads are both 250 kg, and half the sample broke below 250 kg.
Test a larger number of harnesses.
3. A city council wants to know what people think about its recycling centre. It decides to carry out a sample survey of residents.
(a) Write down one reason why the council should not take a census.
Any one of the following. It would take too long, it would be expensive, or the data would be difficult to process.
5. A garage manager wants to know what their mechanics think about a new pension scheme designed for them. The manager asks every mechanic in the garage.
(a) Describe the population the manager will use.
(b) Write down the main advantage of asking all the mechanics.
All the mechanics in the garage.
Every mechanic’s view will be known.

A school has 15 classes and a sixth form. In each class there are 30 students. In the sixth form there are 150 students. There are equal numbers of boys and girls in each class. There are equal numbers of boys and girls in the sixth form. The head teacher wishes to obtain the opinions of the students about school uniforms. Explain how the head teacher would take a stratified sample of size 40.
Number boys and girls separately from 1 to 15 in each class. Choose one of each using random numbers. (B1, B1)
In the sixth form number each group from 1 to 75. Choose five distinct boys and five distinct girls using random numbers. (B1)
You would certainly want to know your mark scheme on this one!
2. A survey is carried out on 100 members of the adult population of a city suburb. The suburb has 2000 residents. An alphabetical list of the inhabitants is available.
(a) Explain one limitation of using a systematic sample.
(b) Describe a sampling method that would be free of bias for this survey.
Taking every 20th person may introduce bias because the sampling frame is in alphabetical order.
Take a simple random sample using the alphabetical list as the sampling frame.
3. A gym wants to take a sample of its members. Each member has a five-digit membership number. The gym selects every member whose number ends in 000.
(a) Is this a systematic sample? Give a reason.
(b) Suggest one way to improve the reliability of this sample.
No. The first person is not selected at random, and the method does not select elements at regular intervals in the membership list.
Use a larger sample to improve reliability. To reduce bias, take a simple random sample using the membership list as the sampling frame.
4. A head of sixth form wants the opinions of Year 12 and Year 13 students about the common room facilities. The table shows the numbers in each year.
(a) Suggest a suitable sampling method for a sample of 40 students.
(b) How many students from each gender in each year should be asked?
students. Round each allocation to the nearest whole number.
5. A factory manager wants to find out how workers travel to work. Each of the 480 workers has a clocking-in number from 1 to 480. Explain how to take a systematic sample of size 30.
Choose a starting number at random from 1 to 16. Select the worker with that clocking-in number, then take every 16th number after it.

6. A sports club director wants a sample of members. Each member has a unique membership number. There are 121 cricket players, 145 hockey players and 104 squash players. No one plays more than one sport.
(a) Explain how to take a simple random sample of 30 and give one disadvantage.
The director decides to take a stratified sample of 30.
(b) State one advantage of this method.
(c) Work out the number of members to select from each sport.
Use the membership list as a sampling frame. Draw 30 distinct numbers by lottery, giving every member the same chance of selection. The sample may not reflect the proportions playing each sport.
Each sport has proportional representation in the sample.
Take 10 cricket, 12 hockey and 8 squash players, giving 30 members.

A lake contains three species of fish. There are estimated to be 1400 trout, 600 bass and 450 pike. A survey of fish health is carried out and a sample of 30 fish is chosen.
(a) Give a reason why stratified random sampling cannot be used. (1)
(b) State an appropriate sampling method for the survey. (1)
(c) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of this method. (2)
(d) Explain how to use this method to select the 30 fish. Show your working. (4)
A sampling frame within each species is impossible to obtain. (B1)
Advantages (B1): quick, low cost or easy to administer.
Disadvantages (B1): sampling errors cannot be estimated, the process is non-random, or species may be difficult to identify.
Catch fish until the quotas of 17 trout, 7 bass and 6 pike are reached. (B1 B1 B1)
Ignore a fish if the quota for its species is full. (B1)
1. Interviewers collect information about spending habits from 40 shoppers in a shopping centre.
(a) Explain how to use (i) quota sampling and (ii) opportunity sampling.
(b) Which method is likely to give a more representative sample?
Divide the population by characteristic. Set each group’s quota in proportion to its size. Identify the group of each interviewee and stop sampling from a group when its quota is full.
Interview those available at the time, for example the first 40 available shoppers.
Quota sampling. An opportunity sample is unlikely to reflect the characteristics of the whole population.
2. Describe the similarities and differences between quota sampling and stratified random sampling.
Both divide the population into groups according to its characteristics. Quota sampling uses non-random selection within groups. Stratified random sampling selects randomly within each stratum.
3. An interviewer asks the first 50 people he sees outside a fish and chip shop on a Friday evening about their eating habits.
(a) What sampling method did he use?
(b) Why might the sample be unrepresentative?
(c) Suggest two improvements to data collection.
Customers at this place and time are unlikely to represent the whole population.
Survey people at different times of day and in other parts of town.
4. A researcher asks the first five people entering a supermarket on Monday morning about their weekly radio listening. They report 4, 7, 6, 8 and 2 hours.
(a) Predict the average weekly hours for the town.
(b) Describe the sampling method and comment on reliability.
This is a small opportunity sample. It is unlikely to represent the town.
Increase the sample size. Ask people at other times or in different locations.
5. Scientists studying the masses of wild deer catch the first five male and the first five female deer they find.
(a) What sampling method are they using?
(c) Compare the masses of male and female deer.
(d) Suggest two improvements to the sampling method.
Any one: no sampling frame is needed, the method is quick, easy or inexpensive, or it allows comparison between males and females.

6. The heights in metres of 20 ostriches are listed below.
(a) Take an opportunity sample of size five.
(b) Starting at the second value, take a systematic sample of five.
(d) State, with reasons, which method is likely to be more reliable.
For example, the first five heights: 1.8, 1.9, 2.3, 1.7, 2.1.
Start at 1.9 and take every fourth height: 1.9, 2.0, 2.6, 2.3, 2.0.
The systematic sample is spread throughout the list and is likely to be more representative. The opportunity sample can include only small values, as it does here.
Can only take specific values, e.g. shoe size, number of children.
Can take any decimal value (possible with a specified range).
Note that while discrete variables only allow specific values, the range could still be infinite, e.g. “number of attempts before success”.

All A Level exam boards are obligated to provide a ‘large data set’. Data in exam questions will often be from this set, and you are encouraged to explore this data (which is publicly available) in Microsoft Excel.
It is important to note that you are expected to be familiar with this data set before you go into your exam, including some basic geographic knowledge!
weather data from a number of weather stations

The median daily total rainfall for the same week in Perth was 19.00mm. Karl states that more southerly countries experience higher rainfall during June. State with a reason whether your answer to part (b) supports this statement.

Perth is in Australia, which is south of the UK, and the median rainfall was higher. However, this is a very small sample from a single location in each country so does not provide enough evidence to support Karl’s statement.

3. Use the sunshine data for the first ten days of June 2015.
(a) Find the mean daily total sunshine for (i) Leeming and (ii) Heathrow.
(b) Find the range for (i) Leeming and (ii) Heathrow.
(c) Supraj says the further north you are, the fewer hours of sunshine. Do your answers support this? Give reasons.
Leeming is further north and has the higher mean sunshine. The data do not support the conclusion. The range does not affect this comparison.
4. Calculate the mean daily total rainfall at Heathrow for the first ten days of June 2015. Explain how you treated 2, 5 and 8 June.
Each “tr” is a trace below 0.05 mm. Treat a trace as zero because it rounds to 0.0 mm to one decimal place.
5. Dominic investigates how average monthly temperature changed during summer 2015 in Jacksonville. He averages temperatures for two days each month and compares the means.
(a) Give one reason two days a month might be (i) a good sample size, (ii) a poor sample size.
(b) He takes the first and last day of each month. Why might this be unrepresentative?
(c) Suggest a better way to choose days.
Sampling from multiple months provides more data.
Two days out of a month of 30 or 31 days is a small sample.
The last day of one month and the first day of the next are consecutive and may share the same weather pattern. The selection is not random.
Number the days and take a simple random sample.
7. Brian calculates mean cloud coverage in Leeming in September 1987 as 9.3 oktas. Explain why this is incorrect.
One okta is one eighth of the sky. Cloud cover cannot exceed 8 oktas, so a mean of 9.3 is impossible.

(a) Describe how to take a systematic sample of 30 days. (3 marks)
(b) Why would this sample not necessarily give 30 data points for her investigation? (1 mark)
